# Investigation of Maternal Outcomes Following Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccination in the Third Trimester: Insights from a Real-World U.S. Electronic Health Records Database

**Authors:** Tina Yi Jin Hsieh; James Cheng-Chung Wei; Ai-ris Collier

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Biomedical Informatics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 2Department of Obstetrics & Gynecology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts | 3Institute of Medicine, Chung Shan Medical University, Taichung, Taiwan | 4Department of Allergy, Immunology & Rheumatology, Chung Shan Medical University Hospital, Taichung, Taiwan | 5Graduate Institute of Integrated Medicine, China Medical University, Taichung, Taiwan | 6Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts. | 7Center for Virology and Vaccine Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts.

## Objective

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises the administration of RSVpreF (Abrysvo), the only authorized bivalent prefusion F respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine for pregnant women, between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation.1, aiming to maximize neonatal immunity during the RSV season (September to January). However, real-world data on post-marketing vaccine uptake remain limited. We aimed to investigate post-vaccination maternal outcomes using real-word data and monitor RSV vaccine uptake changes in the first season in association with other maternal vaccines.

## Study Design

This study queried the TrinetX U.S Collaborative cohort, a real-time federated health research network with electronic health records of around 120 million individuals. We defined the pregnancy cohort by identifying deliveries2 from September 1st, 2023, to April 8th, 2024 (10 weeks after the last date of maternal RSV vaccine recommendation: January 31st, 2024). The geographic distribution of this cohort is 22% Northeast, 15% Midwest, 53% South, and 10% West. The index date was defined as the vaccination date for the RSVpreF group and as 32 to 36 weeks of gestation for the control group. 9.3% received RSVpreF in the cohort. The RSVpreF group patients were more likely to be older, vaccinated with other prenatal vaccines, utilize preventative care, use assisted reproductive technologies, aspirin in pregnancy, and less likely to be hispanic or black (Supplementary Table 1) compared to the control group before PSM. We performed 1:1 propensity score matching based on maternal age, demographics, health utilization, comorbidities, medications, assisted reproductive technology, multi-gestation, multiparity, history of pregnancy complications, social factors, and BMI. Maternal and limited neonatal outcomes (small & large for gestational age) were identified by ICD-10 codes (Supplementary Table 3) and followed-up with a half-year period after the index date. We also delineated the monthly trend in maternal RSVpreF, COVID-19, influenza and Tdap (tetanus diphtheria and acellular pertussis) vaccinations between this period. The Chung Shan Medical University Hospital’s IRB approved the use of TriNetX for this research (CSMUH No: CS2–21176).

## Results

Risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for outcomes were estimated between 6,387 vaccinated and non-vaccinated women. There were no increased risks of preterm birth, gestational hypertensive disorders, gestational diabetes, placental abruption, hemorrhage (ante-,intra-, and postpartum), preterm premature rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, deep vein thrombosis, maternal cardiovascular or neonatal outcomes associated with the maternal RSV vaccination compared to the non-vaccinated cohort (Figure 1-1). The vaccinated group had a slightly lower risk of c-section (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.86–0.96) and oligohydramnios (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.61–0.95) after PSM matching (Supplementary Table 2). RSV vaccination rates rose from September 2023 and peaked in January 2024. Other vaccinations (COVID-19, influenza, and Tdap) followed seasonal trends (Figure 1). Although there was limited vaccination brand data, RSVpreF3 (Arexvy), which is not recommended for the pregnancy population was administered 19 times over seven months, and new RSV vaccines were administered post-1/31/2024, mandating ongoing surveillance. The national RSV vaccination coverage by CDC was 17.8%, compared to 9.3% in our cohort, indicating potential for higher uptake.

## Conclusion

Despite an imbalance in preterm birth in the MATISSE phase 3 trial,3 this multisite US study suggests that maternal RSV vaccine at 32–36-week gestation not associated with an increase in preterm birth. No preterm birth signal was detected in the CDC Vaccine Safety Datalink,4 which samples different regions from TriNetX. There was no increased risk of gestational hypertensive disorders, contrasting with smaller study by Son et al.5 in New York. However, this analysis is limited by the absence of individual patient-level or linked maternal-neonatal data, and lack of granularity for gestational age at vaccination or birth. This analysis does not establish causation, as residual confounding may still be present. RSV vaccination rate rose gradually through the RSV season, peaking in January, before declining, likely as awareness increased during the RSV season. Continued surveillance of real world data is needed to evaluate safety and efficacy in diverse populations.
